bib.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2022 (36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)

read.skipped: References skimmed only; Tables 8, 10, 11 example text skimmed.

question: Can few-shot prompting with intermediate natural-language reasoning steps (a chain of thought) elicit multi-step reasoning in sufficiently large language models without finetuning?
hypothesis: Generating a chain of thought in the few-shot exemplars lets large models decompose multi-step problems and improves arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning, with the effect emerging only at large scale.
contributions: Chain-of-thought prompting: few-shot exemplars of <input, chain of thought, output> triples
Evaluation on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning across LaMDA, GPT-3, PaLM, UL2, Codex
Ablations (equation only, variable compute, CoT after answer) and robustness to annotators, exemplars, order, count
New SOTA on GSM8K with PaLM 540B using 8 exemplars

method.summary: Eight (or four/six) hand-written exemplars with chains of thought are placed in the prompt of off-the-shelf LLMs and answers are decoded greedily; accuracy is compared with standard few-shot prompting across 5 arithmetic, 5 commonsense and 2 symbolic benchmarks. Ablations and annotator/exemplar robustness runs are done mainly on LaMDA 137B.
method.task: multi-step reasoning: arithmetic word problems, commonsense QA, symbolic manipulation

prompts.purpose: Math word problems CoT exemplar (first of 8)
prompts.text:
Q: There are 15 trees in the grove. Grove workers will plant trees in the grove today. After they are done, there will be 21 trees. How many trees did the grove workers plant today?
A: There are 15 trees originally. Then there were 21 trees after some more were planted. So there must have been 21 - 15 = 6. The answer is 6.

Q: Take the last letters of the words in "Elon Musk" and concatenate them.
A: The last letter of "Elon" is "n". The last letter of "Musk" is "k". Concatenating them is "nk". The answer is nk.

Q: A coin is heads up. Maybelle flips the coin. Shalonda does not flip the coin. Is the coin still heads up?
A: The coin was flipped by Maybelle. So the coin was flipped 1 time, which is an odd number. The coin started heads up, so after an odd number of flips, it will be tails up. So the answer is no.

Locations = [counter, table, user, trash, bowl]. Objects = [7up, apple, kettle chips, tea, multigrain chips, coke, lime soda, jalapeno chips, rice chips, orange, grapefruit soda, pepsi, redbull, energy bar, sponge, water]. The robot can pick up items with pick(object) and put down items with put(object) as well as find objects or locations with find(). The robot can only understand the explicit locations and objects listed.

limits: Authors: chain of thought emulates human reasoning but this does not show the network is actually reasoning.
Annotation cost is small for few-shot but could be prohibitive for finetuning.
No guarantee of correct reasoning paths; correct answers can come from wrong chains (1 of 50) and wrong ones from near-correct chains.
Emerges only at large scale (~100B), so costly to serve; CoT hurts most models under 10B.
Gains did not transfer to all models: GPT-3 175B drops on CSQA and StrategyQA.
Prompt engineering still matters: coin flip varies 99.6% to 71.4% across annotators; a list-reversal task could not be prompted by two of three co-authors.
Only greedy decoding; ablations and robustness only on LaMDA 137B due to cost; exemplar-count study on five datasets only.
Model scale is confounded with training compute; GPT-3 sizes are presumed InstructGPT mappings; no compute total estimated.
Dated: arithmetic SOTA and 2022 models (LaMDA, PaLM, text-davinci-002); follow-up work (self-consistency, Wang et al. 2022a) improves on greedy decoding.
